--- title: "Exploring data: into the `tidyverse`" subtitle: "
CMSACamp 2026

Department of Statistics & Data Science
Carnegie Mellon University" footer: "[36-SURE.github.io/2026](https://36-sure.github.io/2026)" format: revealjs: incremental: true theme: theme.scss chalkboard: true smaller: true slide-number: c/t code-line-numbers: false linestretch: 1.5 html-math-method: method: mathjax url: "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/mathjax@3/es5/tex-mml-chtml.js" --- # Data science workflow ## Workflow diagram [![Source: R for Data Science (2e)](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/diagrams/data-science/base.png){width="800"}](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/intro) - **First few lectures:** data wrangling and data visualization - Aspects of data **wrangling**: - **Import:** load in data (e.g., `read_csv()`) - **Tidy:** each row is an observation, each column is a variable (i.e. **tabular** data) - **Transform:** filter observations, create new variables, etc. ## Exploratory data analysis - **Goal of EDA:** perform initial investigations on the data to better understand the data, discover trends/patterns, spot anomalies, etc. . . . - ["EDA is an iterative cycle"](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/EDA.html) - Generate questions about data - Answer via data wrangling and visualization . . . - ["EDA is a state of mind"](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/EDA.html) ::: aside The term EDA was coined by statistician John Tukey in the 1970s. ::: ## Exploratory data analysis - Data can be explored **numerically** (tables, descriptive statistics, etc.) or **visually** (graphs) - Examples of questions: - What type of **variation** do the variables display? - What type of **relationships** exist between variables? . . . - EDA is **NOT** a replacement for statistical inference and learning . . . - EDA is an **important** and **necessary** step to build intuition ## First example: MLB batting statistics **Import** `Batting` table of historical MLB batting statistics from the `Lahman` package. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) # load the tidyverse library(Lahman) # load the Lahman package to access its datasets Batting <- as_tibble(Batting) # initialize the Batting dataset ``` ::: . . . Basic info about the `Batting` dataset: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # number of rows and columns # can also do nrow(Batting) and ncol(Batting) dim(Batting) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 128598 22 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} class(Batting) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "tbl_df" "tbl" "data.frame" ``` ::: ::: ::: aside `tbl` (pronounced "tibble") is the `tidyverse` way of storing tabular data, like a spreadsheet or `data.frame` ::: ## First example: MLB batting statistics **Always look at your data:** view the first 6 (by default) rows with `head()` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # try just typing Batting into your console, what happens? Also try glimpse(Batting) head(Batting) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 6 × 22 playerID yearID stint teamID lgID G AB R H X2B X3B HR 1 aardsda01 2004 1 SFN NL 11 0 0 0 0 0 0 2 aardsda01 2006 1 CHN NL 45 2 0 0 0 0 0 3 aardsda01 2007 1 CHA AL 25 0 0 0 0 0 0 4 aardsda01 2008 1 BOS AL 47 1 0 0 0 0 0 5 aardsda01 2009 1 SEA AL 73 0 0 0 0 0 0 6 aardsda01 2010 1 SEA AL 53 0 0 0 0 0 0 # ℹ 10 more variables: RBI , SB , CS , BB , SO , # IBB , HBP , SH , SF , GIDP ``` ::: ::: . . . Is the `Batting` dataset **tidy**? - Each row = a player's season stint with a team (i.e. players can play for multiple teams in year) - Each column = different measurement or recording about the player-team-season observation (get all column names with `colnames(Batting)` or `names(Batting)`) ## Descriptive statistics We summarize quantitative (e.g. `yearID`, `AB`) and categorical (e.g. `teamID`, `lgID`) variables in different ways . . . - Compute **summary statistics** for quantitative variables with the `summary()` function: . . . ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} summary(Batting$G) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Min. 1st Qu. Median Mean 3rd Qu. Max. 1.0 11.0 31.0 47.3 71.0 165.0 ``` ::: ::: . . . - Compute **counts** of categorical variables with the `table()` function: . . . ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # be careful it ignores NA values! # can do table(Batting$lgID, useNA = "always") table(Batting$lgID) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` AA AL ANL EAS ECL EWL FL IND INT NA NAC NAL NL 1893 54277 154 1035 917 191 472 827 44 737 105 2114 59279 NN2 NNL NSL PL UA WES 2731 2275 237 149 334 827 ``` ::: ::: # Data wrangling with `dplyr` ## The `dplyr` package `dplyr` is a package within the `tidyverse` with functions for data wrangling :::::: columns ::: {.column .fragment width="50%"} ["Grammar of data manipulation"](https://mdsr-book.github.io/mdsr3e/04-dataI.html): - `dplyr` functions are **verbs** - datasets are **nouns** - function arguments are **adverbs** ::: :::: {.column .fragment width="50%"} The six main `dplyr` verbs for data wrangling: ::: nonincremental 1. `filter()` 2. `select()` 3. `arrange()` 4. `mutate()` 5. `group_by()` 6. `summarize()` ::: :::: :::::: ## `filter()` We can use `filter()` to extract **rows** (i.e. observations) that meet certain conditions *Note:* These conditions must be **logical** conditions (aka boolean expressions) ## `filter()` **Example 1:** Extract batting stats for the American League (AL) and National League (NL) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mlb_batting <- filter(Batting, lgID %in% c("AL", "NL")) # or filter(Batting, lgID == "AL" | lgID == "NL") nrow(Batting) - nrow(mlb_batting) # difference in row counts ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 15042 ``` ::: ::: . . .
**Example 2:** Extract batting stats for Pirates players in 2022 ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # multiple conditions pirates_batting <- filter(Batting, yearID == 2022 & teamID == "PIT") head(pirates_batting, n = 3) # difference in row counts ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 22 playerID yearID stint teamID lgID G AB R H X2B X3B HR 1 alforan01 2022 1 PIT NL 2 4 0 1 0 0 0 2 alldrca01 2022 1 PIT NL 1 0 0 0 0 0 0 3 allengr01 2022 1 PIT NL 46 118 17 22 4 0 2 # ℹ 10 more variables: RBI , SB , CS , BB , SO , # IBB , HBP , SH , SF , GIDP ``` ::: ::: ## Logical conditions ::::::: columns :::: {.column .fragment width="50%" style="text-align: left;"} ::: nonincremental - `x < y`: less than - `x <= y`: less than or equal to - `x == y`: equal to - `x != y`: not equal to - `x > y`: greater than - `x >= y`: greater than or equal to ::: :::: :::: {.column .fragment width="50%" style="text-align: left;"} ::: nonincremental - `x %in% y`: whether the value is present in a given vector - `is.na(x)`: is missing - `x & y`: and - `x | y`: or - `!x`: not ::: :::: ::::::: . . .
... and basically anything that returns a TRUE/FALSE value ## Common mistakes ::::: columns ::: {.column .fragment width="50%" style="text-align: left;"} Using `=` instead of `==` nay ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} filter(Batting, team = "PIT") ``` ::: yay ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} filter(Batting, team == "PIT") ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column .fragment width="50%" style="text-align: left;"} Forgetting quotes (for string/character) nay ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} filter(Batting, team == PIT) ``` ::: yay ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} filter(Batting, team == "PIT") ``` ::: ::: ::::: ## `select()` We can use `select()` to extract **columns** (variables) of interest *We simply specify the column names:* ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} select(Batting, playerID, yearID, G, AB, R, H, HR, BB) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 128,598 × 8 playerID yearID G AB R H HR BB 1 aardsda01 2004 11 0 0 0 0 0 2 aardsda01 2006 45 2 0 0 0 0 3 aardsda01 2007 25 0 0 0 0 0 4 aardsda01 2008 47 1 0 0 0 0 5 aardsda01 2009 73 0 0 0 0 0 6 aardsda01 2010 53 0 0 0 0 0 7 aardsda01 2012 1 0 0 0 0 0 8 aardsda01 2013 43 0 0 0 0 0 9 aardsda01 2015 33 1 0 0 0 0 10 aaronha01 1954 122 468 58 131 13 28 # ℹ 128,588 more rows ``` ::: ::: ## `mutate()` We use `mutate()` to create new variables - New variables created via `mutate()` are usually based on existing variables - Make sure to give your new variable a name - Naming the new variable the same as the existing variable will overwrite the original column . . . **Example:** Get the batting average and strikeout-to-walk ratio for every player ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} new_batting <- mutate(Batting, batting_avg = H / AB, so_bb_ratio = SO / BB) head(new_batting, n = 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 24 playerID yearID stint teamID lgID G AB R H X2B X3B HR 1 aardsda01 2004 1 SFN NL 11 0 0 0 0 0 0 # ℹ 12 more variables: RBI , SB , CS , BB , SO , # IBB , HBP , SH , SF , GIDP , batting_avg , # so_bb_ratio ``` ::: ::: ## `arrange()` We use `arrange()` to sort the observations (rows) by variables (columns) . . . *Default is ascending order:* ::: nonincremental - Low to high for numeric columns - Alphabetical order for character columns ::: . . . **Example 1:** Who holds the single-season home run record? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hr_batting <- arrange(Batting, desc(HR)) # desc() for descending order head(hr_batting, n = 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 22 playerID yearID stint teamID lgID G AB R H X2B X3B HR 1 bondsba01 2001 1 SFN NL 153 476 129 156 32 2 73 2 mcgwima01 1998 1 SLN NL 155 509 130 152 21 0 70 3 sosasa01 1998 1 CHN NL 159 643 134 198 20 0 66 # ℹ 10 more variables: RBI , SB , CS , BB , SO , # IBB , HBP , SH , SF , GIDP ``` ::: ::: ## `arrange()` **Example 2:** we can arrange by multiple columns at once: ::: nonincremental 1. At bats from high to low 2. Home runs from low to high ::: . . . *Variable order matters!*
. . . ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ab_hr_batting <- arrange(Batting, desc(AB), HR) head(ab_hr_batting, n = 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 22 playerID yearID stint teamID lgID G AB R H X2B X3B HR 1 rolliji01 2007 1 PHI NL 162 716 139 212 38 20 30 2 wilsowi02 1980 1 KCA AL 161 705 133 230 28 15 3 3 suzukic01 2004 1 SEA AL 161 704 101 262 24 5 8 # ℹ 10 more variables: RBI , SB , CS , BB , SO , # IBB , HBP , SH , SF , GIDP ``` ::: ::: ## Performing multiple operations What if we want to perform **several** tasks using multiple `dplyr` verbs? . . .
**Example:** Which Pirates players had the highest batting average in 2022, among those with at least 50 at bats? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} select(arrange(mutate(filter(Batting, yearID == 2022, teamID == "PIT", AB >= 50), batting_avg = H / AB), desc(batting_avg)), playerID, AB, batting_avg) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 23 × 3 playerID AB batting_avg 1 newmake01 288 0.274 2 reynobr01 542 0.262 3 hayeske01 505 0.244 4 marisja01 77 0.234 5 perezro02 60 0.233 6 castrro01 253 0.233 7 cruzon01 331 0.233 8 gamelbe01 371 0.232 9 chavimi01 401 0.229 10 vogelda01 237 0.228 # ℹ 13 more rows ``` ::: ::: . . . *That's awfully annoying to write, and also difficult to read...* ## The pipe operator Introducing the **pipe operator** `|>` . . .
*Note:* You might have seen the `magrittr` pipe `%>%`... - This is from the `maggritr` package, automatically loaded when loading `tidyverse` - Recently, many people (including Hadley Wickham) have switched to `|>`, the built-in "native" pipe to base `R` - [While identical in many ways, there are some differences](https://www.tidyverse.org/blog/2023/04/base-vs-magrittr-pipe/) ::: aside Shortcut for the pipe operator in RStudio: Command (or Ctrl) + Shift + M ::: ## The pipe operator ::: nonincremental - We use `|>` to perform a sequence of operations (think of as: "and then...") - The pipe takes an object (e.g., tibble, data frame, matrix, vector) on the left and passes it as the first argument of the function on the right ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # the workflow object |> first_operation(...) |> second_operation(...) |> . . . last_operation(...) ``` ::: ## Performing multiple operations **Recall our example:** Which Pirates players had the highest batting average in 2022, among those with at least 50 at bats? . . .
**Our list of tasks:** . . . :::{.nonincremental} - `filter()`: only Pirates players in 2022 with at least 50 at bats - `mutate()`: create a new column for batting average - `arrange()`: sort by batting average in descending order - `select()`: report player name, at bats, and batting average ::: ## Performing multiple operations ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} Batting |> filter(yearID == 2022, teamID == "PIT", AB >= 50) |> mutate(batting_avg = H / AB) |> arrange(desc(batting_avg)) |> select(playerID, AB, batting_avg) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 23 × 3 playerID AB batting_avg 1 newmake01 288 0.274 2 reynobr01 542 0.262 3 hayeske01 505 0.244 4 marisja01 77 0.234 5 perezro02 60 0.233 6 castrro01 253 0.233 7 cruzon01 331 0.233 8 gamelbe01 371 0.232 9 chavimi01 401 0.229 10 vogelda01 237 0.228 # ℹ 13 more rows ``` ::: ::: . . . *This is much easier to write and read!* ## `summarize()` (by itself) We use `summarize()` to collapse the data down to a single row (per group) by aggregating variables into single values *This is useful for computing summaries (e.g., mean, median, max, min, correlation)* . . . **Example 1:** Extracting the median at bats ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} Batting |> summarize(median_at_bats = median(AB)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 1 median_at_bats 1 40 ``` ::: ::: . . . **Example 2:** Extracting the correlation between at bats and home runs ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} Batting |> summarize(cor_ab_hr = cor(AB, HR)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 1 cor_ab_hr 1 0.712 ``` ::: ::: ## `group_by()` and `summarize()` We can use `group_by()` to covert the data into a "grouped tbl", where operations are performed by group - That is, `group_by()` splits the data into groups based on column values - Powerful when combined with `summarize()` - After the operation is done at the group-level, you may have to use `ungroup()` to remove leftover groupings . . . ## `group_by()` and `summarize()` **Example:** How many home runs, strike outs, and walks did each team accumulate in each season from 2015 to 2019? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} Batting |> filter(yearID %in% 2015:2019) |> group_by(teamID) |> summarize(total_hr = sum(HR), total_so = sum(SO), total_bb = sum(BB)) |> arrange(desc(total_hr)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 30 × 4 teamID total_hr total_so total_bb 1 NYA 1209 6659 2839 2 HOU 1159 6294 2759 3 TOR 1139 6741 2752 4 LAN 1111 6751 2991 5 BAL 1103 6914 2162 6 TEX 1041 7008 2572 7 SEA 1036 6693 2489 8 MIN 1035 6694 2604 9 OAK 1033 6474 2610 10 MIL 1031 7434 2724 # ℹ 20 more rows ``` ::: ::: # The lesser-known stars of `dplyr` ## `count()` `count()` returns the number of observations in each group ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} Batting |> count(lgID, name = "freq") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 19 × 2 lgID freq 1 AA 1893 2 AL 54277 3 ANL 154 4 EAS 1035 5 ECL 917 6 EWL 191 7 FL 472 8 IND 827 9 INT 44 10 NA 737 11 NAC 105 12 NAL 2114 13 NL 59279 14 NN2 2731 15 NNL 2275 16 NSL 237 17 PL 149 18 UA 334 19 WES 827 ``` ::: ::: ## Alternatives to `count()` ::::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} Using `group_by()` and `summarize()` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # note: count is a "shortcut" of this Batting |> group_by(lgID) |> summarize(freq = n()) |> ungroup() ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} Using Base R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # recall that in base R... table(Batting$lgID) ``` ::: ::: ::::: ## `slice_*()` family for subsetting rows ::: nonincremental `slice()`: extract rows (observations) based on the row index ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} Batting |> slice(c(1, 99, 101, 500)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 4 × 22 playerID yearID stint teamID lgID G AB R H X2B X3B HR 1 aardsda01 2004 1 SFN NL 11 0 0 0 0 0 0 2 abbotfr01 1904 1 CLE AL 41 130 14 22 4 2 0 3 abbotgl01 1973 1 OAK AL 5 0 0 0 0 0 0 4 adamsbo03 1951 1 CIN NL 125 403 57 107 12 5 5 # ℹ 10 more variables: RBI , SB , CS , BB , SO , # IBB , HBP , SH , SF , GIDP ``` ::: ::: ## `slice_*()` family for subsetting rows ::: nonincremental `slice_head()` / `slice_tail()`: extract the first / last `n` rows ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Batting |> slice_tail(n = 5) Batting |> slice_head(n = 5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 22 playerID yearID stint teamID lgID G AB R H X2B X3B HR 1 aardsda01 2004 1 SFN NL 11 0 0 0 0 0 0 2 aardsda01 2006 1 CHN NL 45 2 0 0 0 0 0 3 aardsda01 2007 1 CHA AL 25 0 0 0 0 0 0 4 aardsda01 2008 1 BOS AL 47 1 0 0 0 0 0 5 aardsda01 2009 1 SEA AL 73 0 0 0 0 0 0 # ℹ 10 more variables: RBI , SB , CS , BB , SO , # IBB , HBP , SH , SF , GIDP ``` ::: ::: ## `slice_*()` family for subsetting rows ::: nonincremental `slice_min()` / `slice_max()`: extract rows with the smallest or largest values of a variable ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # single-season home run record (top 5) Batting |> slice_max(HR, n = 5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 22 playerID yearID stint teamID lgID G AB R H X2B X3B HR 1 bondsba01 2001 1 SFN NL 153 476 129 156 32 2 73 2 mcgwima01 1998 1 SLN NL 155 509 130 152 21 0 70 3 sosasa01 1998 1 CHN NL 159 643 134 198 20 0 66 4 mcgwima01 1999 1 SLN NL 153 521 118 145 21 1 65 5 sosasa01 2001 1 CHN NL 160 577 146 189 34 5 64 # ℹ 10 more variables: RBI , SB , CS , BB , SO , # IBB , HBP , SH , SF , GIDP ``` ::: ::: ## `slice_*()` family for subsetting rows `slice_sample()`: randomly sample a specified number / fraction of observation in the data ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # randomly sample 1000 rows (without replacement, by default) Batting |> slice_sample(n = 1000) # randomly sample 70% of the rows, with replacement Batting |> slice_sample(prop = 0.7, replace = TRUE) ``` :::
*Useful for performing resampling (e.g., bootstrap, cross-validation, etc.)* ## Putting it all together (pt. 2) **Example 1:** Get batting stats for each year: each row is a year with the following variables ::: nonincremental - total hits, home runs, strikeouts, walks, atbats - total batting average for each year = total H / total AB - only keeps AL and NL leagues ::: . . . ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} yearly_batting <- Batting |> filter(lgID %in% c("AL", "NL")) |> group_by(yearID) |> summarize(total_h = sum(H, na.rm = TRUE), total_hr = sum(HR, na.rm = TRUE), total_so = sum(SO, na.rm = TRUE), total_bb = sum(BB, na.rm = TRUE), total_ab = sum(AB, na.rm = TRUE)) |> mutate(batting_avg = total_h / total_ab) ``` ::: ## Putting it all together (pt. 2) **Example 2:** What are the top three years with the most HRs? . . . ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} yearly_batting |> slice_max(total_hr, n = 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 7 yearID total_h total_hr total_so total_bb total_ab batting_avg 1 2019 42039 6776 42823 15895 166651 0.252 2 2017 42215 6105 40104 15829 165567 0.255 3 2021 39484 5944 42145 15794 161941 0.244 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # or this yearly_batting |> arrange(desc(total_hr)) |> slice(1:3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 7 yearID total_h total_hr total_so total_bb total_ab batting_avg 1 2019 42039 6776 42823 15895 166651 0.252 2 2017 42215 6105 40104 15829 165567 0.255 3 2021 39484 5944 42145 15794 161941 0.244 ``` ::: ::: ## Putting it all together (pt. 2) **Example 3:** Which years have the best and worst strikeout to walk ratios? . . . ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} yearly_batting |> mutate(so_bb_ratio = total_so / total_bb) |> arrange(so_bb_ratio) |> slice(c(1, n())) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 8 yearID total_h total_hr total_so total_bb total_ab batting_avg so_bb_ratio 1 1893 15913 460 3341 6143 56898 0.280 0.544 2 1879 6171 58 1843 508 24155 0.255 3.63 ``` ::: ::: ## We can make better looking tables Using `rename()` and `gt()`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(gt) yearly_batting |> select(yearID, batting_avg) |> rename(Year = yearID, `Batting Average` = batting_avg) |> arrange(desc(`Batting Average`)) |> slice(c(1:3, (n()-2):n())) |> gt() |> fmt_number(columns = `Batting Average`, decimals = 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
Year Batting Average
1894 0.309
1895 0.296
1930 0.296
1908 0.239
1888 0.239
1968 0.237
``` ::: ::: ## Lots of ways to customize tables with `gt()` ::: {.cell output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} yearly_batting |> select(yearID, batting_avg) |> rename(Year = yearID, `Batting Average` = batting_avg) |> arrange(desc(`Batting Average`)) |> slice(c(1:3, (n()-2):n())) |> gt(rowname_col = "Year") |> # add table header tab_header(title = "Best / Worst MLB Seasons by Batting Average") |> # create row groups by location tab_row_group( label = "Bottom 3 Years", rows = 4:6 ) |> tab_row_group( label = "Top 3 Years", rows = 1:3 ) |> # recolor row group labels tab_style( style = cell_fill(color = "bisque"), locations = cells_row_groups(groups = "Bottom 3 Years") ) |> tab_style( style = cell_fill(color = "darkseagreen1"), locations = cells_row_groups(groups = "Top 3 Years")) |> # round "Batting Average" to 3 decimals fmt_number(columns = `Batting Average`, decimals = 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
Best / Worst MLB Seasons by Batting Average
Batting Average
Top 3 Years
1894 0.309
1895 0.296
1930 0.296
Bottom 3 Years
1908 0.239
1888 0.239
1968 0.237
``` ::: ::: . . . ::: {style="text-align: center;"} *Enough with tables (for now)!* ::: ## What's next? ::::: columns ::: {.column width="50%" style="text-align: left;"} **DATA VISUALIZATION** > The simple graph has brought more information to the data analyst’s mind than any other device. — John Tukey - Use `ggplot2` (and the grammar of graphics) to visually explore data - More intuitive than base `R` plotting - Different types of visualizations for categorical and quantitative data, faceting, etc. - `dplyr` verbs and `|>` leads to natural pipeline for EDA ::: ::: {.column width="50%" style="text-align: center;"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](01-explore_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-36-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ::: ::::: ## See you later, partner ![[A "data wrangler" illustration of the `dplyr` package, courtesy of Allison Horst](https://allisonhorst.shinyapps.io/dplyr-learnr/)](/images/data-wrangler.png){width="750" fig-align="center"}

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
